vocab.definition: A conversation about a role and what you can offer.
A real event or action that shows a skill.
Information that helps you improve your work.
Ask or explain so the meaning is clear.
Try again using what you have learnt.
Help that lets you take part.

cases.text: A question is unclear. The learner asks for it to be explained.
cases.fact: Understanding the question comes before answering.
cases.next_step: Repeat it in plain words and give thinking time.
cases.staff_note: Do not treat asking for help as failure.

cases.text: An answer says: I am good at all jobs. It gives no example.
cases.fact: There is no action to link to a skill.
cases.next_step: Ask for one real task and the learner’s own part in it.
cases.staff_note: Do not supply an invented work history.

cases.text: A learner describes how they checked class kit against a list.
cases.fact: Checking is one task in the made-up role.
cases.next_step: Ask what they did and what happened next.
cases.staff_note: Class experience can be relevant; name its context honestly.

cases.text: Feedback says: Add what you did next. The learner tries the answer again.
cases.fact: The second answer can make the action clearer.
cases.next_step: Keep the actual first answer, prompt and revised answer.
cases.staff_note: A blank retry box is not evidence that a response happened.

cases.text: A learner uses their usual aid and takes time to respond.
cases.fact: The aid supports the learner to express their own meaning.
cases.next_step: Listen to the content and record the support used.
cases.staff_note: No forced eye contact, handshake, speed or public performance.

cases.text: A question asks about a task the learner has never done.
cases.fact: No example exists for that exact task.
cases.next_step: Say so; offer a related true example or a next learning step.
cases.staff_note: Never fill the gap with a fictional achievement.

You Do practice: 12 minutes.
Teacher: Read the fictional role and model one answer. For 12 minutes, use the three question cards in an adult-led or willing pair exchange; offer one question as a supported entry. Give one specific prompt after the first answer and allow a retry. Each learner keeps their own two-page record. The six-minute capture preserves real words, support, response and any unattempted question. Do not fill gaps from the adult model.

Boundaries

Use learner ID and role labels. Do not ask about private health, family, contact details or personal trauma. No forced pair work, eye contact, handshake or filmed performance. Assessment and feedback

The core evidence is an actual question-and-answer exchange and feedback response, not merely a completed script. Record the question and exact words or a faithful work reference. Check the example is authentic and relevant to the fictional role. Preserve the first answer, a specific feedback prompt and the learner’s retry. If no retry occurs, record not yet and the planned support. Week 4 is formative rehearsal; Week 7 is the assessing lesson. No job offer or award completion is claimed.

Retain actual work, response mode and support. Use VF · WS · I · NS+ (Yellow Box) · // (self-edit) · ? (read back) · R (responded) · E (evidence in the school’s evidence record). R requires Voice, Audience, an NS+ prompt and the learner’s response in their own colour. Record E only after evidence is banked. Blank forms and adult models are not completed learner evidence.
Learner voice
Space: calm, accessible participation. Voice: a choice, reason or help request. Audience: the adult listens or reads and replies. Influence: record the support or next-step change made in response.
Offer to the Communication portfolio

Listen to a question, ask for clarification, give a relevant answer and respond to specific feedback. The receiving teacher maps authentic responses to their own portfolio; no communication criteria are assigned here.

Model and hinge

Adult model: Tell me how you check work. I had to sort class kit by its label. I checked each item against a short list. I found one item in the wrong place. Feedback: explain what you did next. Retry: I moved it, then checked the list again.

Individual evidence key

The core evidence is an actual question-and-answer exchange and feedback response, not merely a completed script. Record the question and exact words or a faithful work reference. Check the example is authentic and relevant to the fictional role. Preserve the first answer, a specific feedback prompt and the learner’s retry. Feedback boundaries and next teaching
Card A: Do not treat asking for help as failure.
Card B: Do not supply an invented work history.
Card C: Class experience can be relevant; name its context honestly.
Card D: A blank retry box is not evidence that a response happened.
Card E: No forced eye contact, handshake, speed or public performance.
Card F: Never fill the gap with a fictional achievement.
Common misunderstandings

An interview is a two-way conversation. A short, relevant answer can show a skill. Reading from notes or using a communication aid is a valid support. Feedback should point to a change in the answer, not judge personality, eye contact or confidence. Practising does not guarantee a job.
Teaching boundary

Use learner ID and role labels. Do not ask about private health, family, contact details or personal trauma. No forced pair work, eye contact, handshake or filmed performance. The learner may pause, use notes or usual communication support. Record actual participation and any gap, without inferring confidence, ability or attainment from speaking style.

If a reason is missing, return to the fact or actual work. Re-model a different example, then keep the learner’s own revision. Use NS+ and the learner response in their own colour before R. E means evidence actually banked. Keep safeguarding records separate.
